name: Sauternes

climate.koppen_name: Temperate, no dry season, warm summer

terms: France's protected place names. A wine sold under one must follow that appellation's rules. The EU's term for the same tier is PDO, or AOP in French.
Indication Géographique Protégée, the tier below AOC. It replaced vin de pays in 2009.
France's simplest category, in use since 2010. It replaced vin de table.
There is no legal or agreed definition of old, so the words promise nothing on their own.
One of the two regional appellations allowed anywhere in Bordeaux, beside plain Bordeaux. Together they cover about half the Bordeaux vineyard.

In 1855 brokers ranked Bordeaux estates by reputation and price. Reds were ranked from first to fifth growths, nearly all in the Médoc, and the sweet whites of Sauternes and Barsac from superior first growth to second growth.
Botrytis cinerea, a fungus that in warm, humid weather can turn grapes into fine, concentrated sweet wine.
keyfacts: Sauternes is a sweet white wine made from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris and Muscadelle grapes affected by Botrytis cinerea, also called noble rot.
Where the Ciron meets the Garonne, condensation brings humid nights, and drying sun and wind by day favor noble rot.
Grapes are picked by hand in successive passes, selecting the botrytized berries, and yields vary widely between vintages.
In the 1855 classification, Château d'Yquem alone was ranked Premier Cru Supérieur, above 11 Premiers Crus and 15 Deuxièmes Crus.
Five communes may use the name Sauternes: Barsac, Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues and Preignac, and Barsac may also use its own appellation.

notes: Sauternes is a sweet white from grapes touched by noble rot, and it must taste noticeably sweet.
It balances sweetness with zesty acidity.
Common notes are apricot, honey and peach, with a nutty note typical of botrytized Sémillon.
The best can age well beyond 100 years.
In years without noble rot, producers often make dry whites sold as Bordeaux AOC.

blurb.text: A Bordeaux appellation within Sauternes & Barsac for sweet white wine from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle affected by noble rot (Botrytis cinerea). Its climate often brings noble rot, though harvests vary widely between vintages.
